Sending money home with stablecoins: how it works, what it costs and what can go wrong

Some people send money to family abroad with stablecoins instead of a transfer service. It can be quicker or cheaper in some cases, but it adds new risks, so check carefully before you try.

How it works

  1. The sender buys a stablecoin on a platform that is allowed in the sender's country.
  2. The sender sends it to the receiver's wallet or account, on a network that both sides agreed on.
  3. The receiver converts it to local money, for example through a local platform or a P2P market.
  4. The receiver cashes out, often to a bank account or mobile money.

Costs to compare

  • The fee or spread when buying the stablecoin.
  • The network fee for the transfer, which depends on the network you choose.
  • The exchange rate when converting to local money. P2P offers can differ a lot from each other.
  • The fee for cashing out to a bank or mobile money.
  • Compare the total, not only one step, with what a normal transfer service would charge.

Safe habits

  1. Agree the network and address by voice or video with someone you know, not only by text.
  2. Send a small test amount first and wait until it arrives.
  3. Check the address by comparing the first and last characters, and copy it instead of typing it.
  4. Use only platforms that are legal and available in both countries.
  5. Keep records: screenshots, transaction IDs and dates. They help with disputes and with tax rules.

What can go wrong

  • Wrong network. If the network does not match, the money can be lost.
  • P2P scams. Fake proof of payment, or a buyer who reverses a bank payment after you release the coins.
  • Rules and limits. Many countries have limits, reporting rules or restrictions on crypto, and they differ for sender and receiver.
  • Price moves. Even a stablecoin can drift from its price. See the stablecoin guide.
  • Frozen accounts. A platform or bank may freeze an account it considers suspicious.

Is it right for you?

For small, regular amounts it may be cheaper, but only if the rules in both countries allow it and both people are comfortable with wallets. If anything is unclear, a licensed transfer service may be safer. This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Tools mentioned in this guide

  • CoinGecko

    Prices, market caps and basic data for thousands of coins.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open the CoinGecko website and type the token's name or ticker in the search box.
    2. Pick the result with the right name and symbol. Fake tokens copy names, so compare the contract address on the page with the one the project publishes on its own website.
    3. Look at market cap, 24-hour trading volume and the number of markets. Very low volume, or one tiny market, means a single trade can move the price.
    4. Use the official website and social links listed on the token page, not links sent to you in a chat.
    5. Open the price chart with the longest range to see the whole history, and check which exchanges list the token.

    CoinGecko shows data. It does not tell you whether a token is safe or will rise.

    Level: Beginner
    Open CoinGecko (opens in a new tab)

  • GoPlus Security

    Checks tokens, contracts and links for common scam and honeypot risks.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open the GoPlus website and find its token security checker.
    2. Choose the blockchain network the token lives on, such as Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana or TRON.
    3. Paste the contract address. Copy it from the project's official website or from CoinGecko, not from a chat message, then run the check.
    4. Read the warnings first: honeypot (you can buy but not sell), very high buy or sell tax, an owner who can mint new tokens or change the rules, and hidden owners.
    5. If the report shows several risks, do not buy or approve anything. If it looks clean, remember that is only one input.

    A clean scan is not a guarantee. New scams are built to pass checks, and the tool cannot see the team's plans.

    Level: Beginner
    Open GoPlus Security (opens in a new tab)
